doc.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Management pressure to fire Dizzy at the Famous Door
summary: Carter ignored club owner Irving Alexander's dislike of Gillespie's music and kept him on.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk

blocks.x: No, okay. You had mentioned before that you were under some pressure at one point to dismiss Dizzy, by management.
Oh, well, that was later when we worked together at the Famous Door. The . . . what’s his name, the . . . Irving Alexander, I think was the guy, and he didn’t understand Dizzy’s music, you know.
How did you handle that? You didn’t get rid of him, obviously. How did you handle the . . .
Oh, no, he probably left at some time because he, you know, had better paying offers, so I handled it by just ignoring the guy and keeping him on.
Was Dizzy aware of this pressure that . . .

I don’t know. I think a lot of people looked askance at what he was doing, and I think he just went along with the flow and ignored it and all; did his thing, you know. And he’s still doing his thing, as I said.
What about the audience? Do you remember how he was received? Was there any skepticism visible in the people that came to the club?
I don’t remember that. I don’t think so.
Nobody threw tomatoes at him or . . .
Oh, no, indeed not. No, indeed not. I think everyone thought they were, you know, witnessing something new, which we all were.
Did you play trumpet with him at all during that . . .
